questions.question: What is SPI?

options.A: A percentage that shows only how many classes you attended.
options.B: A skill score from 0 to 10 that reflects how consistently you learn, how you take part in assessments, and how well you master skills.
options.C: A rank that compares your marks with other students in your batch.
options.D: A grade (A+ to F) given only for your Final Skill Assessment.

explanation: SPI is a skill score from 0 to 10. It looks at three things together: continuous learning, assessment participation and skill mastery. It is not a rank or a single exam grade.
Every course gets its own score, and these combine into your overall SPI.

questions.question: How are you assessed in a course under SPI?

options.A: One Final Skill Assessment at the end of the course; everything before it is just practice.
options.B: Two checkpoints: a mid-course exam and a final exam.
options.C: Four checkpoints that build up through the course: Classroom Quizzes, Module Quizzes, Skill Assessments and one Final Skill Assessment.
options.D: Weekly tests in every course, with no final assessment.

explanation: Your learning is checked at four levels, not only at the end.
• Classroom Quizzes (2 per topic) check topic-level clarity.
• Module Quizzes (every 3 topics) check how you apply concepts across a module.
• Skill Assessments (every 15–30 days) check speed, accuracy and retention.
• The Final Skill Assessment (once, at the end of the course) checks full skill readiness.
Every checkpoint counts, so your SPI is built from day one.

questions.question: How do the assessments contribute to your course score?

options.A: Each carries a different weight. The Final Skill Assessment carries the most (50%), and you need at least 50% in every component to get SPI.
options.B: All four carry equal weight, 25% each.
options.C: Classroom Quizzes carry the most weight because you take them most often.
options.D: Skill Assessments carry the most weight at 50%.

explanation: The weights are Classroom Quizzes 10%, Module Quizzes 15%, Skill Assessments 25% and Final Skill Assessment 50%. For example, averages of 80, 80, 72 and 88 give a course score of 82 out of 100.
The Final Skill Assessment moves your score the most, but it cannot carry you alone. You must score at least 50% in each component to get SPI.

questions.question: How does your course score turn into SPI points?

options.A: Your score is divided by 10 to give your points.
options.B: Every pass earns 10 points and every fail earns 0.
options.C: Points are the average of your attendance and quiz scores.
options.D: Your score falls in a level band (A+ to F), and each level earns fixed points. F (below 50%) and Ab (absent) earn 0 points.

explanation: Your score maps to a level, and each level earns fixed points:
• 90–100 → Level A+ → 10 points
• 80–89.99 → Level A → 9 points
• 70–79.99 → Level B → 8 points
• 60–69.99 → Level C → 7 points
• 50–59.99 → Level D → 6 points
• Below 50 → Level F → 0 points
• Absent → Level Ab → 0 points
A course score of 82 is Level A, which earns 9 points. Scoring 49% earns 0 points, not 4.9. An F or Ab also turns the course into a Skill Debt.

questions.question: How is your overall SPI for a skill cycle calculated?

options.A: Take the simple average of the points of all courses.
options.B: Multiply each course's points by its weight, add them up, and divide by the total of the weights.
options.C: Add up the points of all courses.
options.D: Take the points of your best course.

explanation: SPI = Sum of (Course Points × Weights) ÷ Total Weights. For example, a weighted total of 165 divided by total weights of 20 gives 8.25 out of 10.
Higher-weighted courses pull your SPI more, so a low result in a high-weight course hurts more than in a low-weight one.

questions.question: Which of these is required to earn your SPI?

options.A: Minimum 60% attendance and an attempt at the Final Skill Assessment.
options.B: A high Final Skill Assessment score, which makes up for missed quizzes and low attendance.
options.C: Minimum 80% attendance, full participation in every assessment (the Final Skill Assessment is mandatory), and no malpractice cases.
options.D: Minimum 80% attendance alone; taking part in assessments is optional.

explanation: You earn SPI only when every requirement is met:
• at least 80% attendance
• 100% participation in Classroom Quizzes and Skill Assessments
• 100% completion of Module Quizzes
• the Final Skill Assessment, which is mandatory
• no malpractice cases
If even one is missing, you do not get SPI, however well you score elsewhere.

questions.question: You miss classes and your attendance drops below 80%. What happens?

options.A: You are placed in Recovery Mode and must attend assigned recovery classes to get back to 80% and catch up on the missed topics.
options.B: Watching the recordings of the missed classes removes the absence.
options.C: Nothing happens as long as you pass the assessments.
options.D: Your SPI is reduced slightly and you carry on as usual.

explanation: A missed class counts as absent. Watching the recording helps you catch up on content but does not undo the absence. Recovery Mode is a mandatory way to catch up, not a punishment.
• Recovery classes are scheduled outside regular college hours.
• They are compulsory and tracked like a normal class, with camera on if online.
• Once you reach 80% again, you are back to normal and all benefits reopen.

If you skip recovery classes, you will not be allowed to sit the assessment, and the course is automatically marked as Skill Debt. For a genuine medical or emergency reason, inform your mentor and submit valid proof within 5 days.

questions.question: You get an F in a course, so it becomes a Skill Debt. What does an active Skill Debt mean for you?

options.A: Only that course's SPI is affected; everything else continues as normal.
options.B: Only placement drives are blocked; internships and other activities stay open.
options.C: You can continue all activities, but with lower priority.
options.D: You cannot take part in any NIAT-specific activities (MINT, BRAVE, GRIT, placements, internships, co-curricular support) until it is cleared.

explanation: Even a single Skill Debt puts all of these on hold until it is cleared. A Skill Debt is created by an F (below 50%) or Ab (absent) in a course, or by skipping recovery classes.
You must clear all Skill Debts within the next cycle, or face a review that could lead to program extension or discontinuation.

questions.question: What should you do to clear a Skill Debt?

options.A: Nothing, it clears automatically when the cycle ends.
options.B: Attend the recovery classes, finish the pending work, and re-attempt the Final Skill Assessment for that course, all within the next cycle.
options.C: Just re-sit the Final Skill Assessment; recovery classes and pending work are optional.
options.D: Carry it forward; there is no time limit as long as you attend regular classes.

explanation: Skill Debt courses are auto-enrolled into the recovery window. The path has four steps:
1. Recovery window
2. Attend recovery classes
3. Finish pending assignments, module assessments or practice work
4. Re-attempt the Final Skill Assessment for that course

For a medical or emergency reason, submit proof within 5 days to re-sit as a first attempt, with no grade cap and no fee. If you have 2 or more F/Ab grades, counselling with your mentor is mandatory before you restart, and a recovery plan is tracked.

questions.question: Two students work together on their answers during a Skill Assessment without permission. How does NIAT treat this?

options.A: It is fine as long as both write their own final answers.
options.B: A warning the first time, and they can retake in the same cycle.
options.C: It is a breach: the course result is reset to fail, with no retake in that skill cycle.
options.D: Only a small mark deduction for that assessment.

explanation: NIAT has zero tolerance for cheating, plagiarism, fabricating data, unauthorised collaboration and falsifying records. The consequences are:
• the course result is reset to fail, with no retake that skill cycle (you repeat it when it reopens)
• removal from any official position or title at NIAT
• exclusion from external PR activities
Malpractice also makes you ineligible to earn SPI.
